samf-junior-2000-r2-01.title: Last digits only
samf-junior-2000-r2-01.body:
Only the last digits matter: $1\times3\times5=15$, which ends in 5. (Indeed $11\times13\times15=2145$.)

**Answer: (C) 5**

samf-junior-2000-r2-03.title: Estimate
samf-junior-2000-r2-03.body:
$2.001\div2.000\approx1$ and $1.999\approx2$, so the fraction is about $\frac{1}{2}$: (precisely, $\frac{1.0005}{1.999}\approx0.5005$).

**Answer: (D) $\frac12$**

samf-junior-2000-r2-04.title: Differences stay the same
samf-junior-2000-r2-04.body:
The difference of denominator and numerator stays $11-8=3$. A fraction equivalent to $\frac23$ with difference 3 is $\frac69$. So the numerator went from 8 to 6: the number subtracted is 2.

**Answer: (B) 2**

samf-junior-2000-r2-05.title: Divisibility
samf-junior-2000-r2-05.body:
$x$ divides $100-2=98$, and since the remainder is 2, $x>2$. Then $198=2\times98+2=2\times 98 + 2$, so $198\equiv2\pmod x$: the remainder is 2.

**Answer: (B) 2**

samf-junior-2000-r2-06.title: Volume over base area
samf-junior-2000-r2-06.body:
In one minute 2 litres $=2000\text{ cm}^3$ enter. The base is $100\text{ cm}\times100\text{ cm}=10\,000\text{ cm}^2$, so the level rises $\frac{2000}{10000}=0.2$ cm each minute.

**Answer: (B) 0.2 cm/min**

samf-junior-2000-r2-07.title: Count paths to each point
samf-junior-2000-r2-07.body:
Let each vertex record the number of ways to reach it from A. The two upper side vertices get 1 each. The centre can be reached from A, and from both upper side vertices: $1+1+1=3$. Each lower side vertex is reached from the upper vertex above it and from the centre: $1+3=4$. Finally B is reached from the two lower side vertices and from the centre: $4+4+3=11$.

**Answer: (C) 11**

samf-junior-2000-r2-08.title: By digit sum
samf-junior-2000-r2-08.body:
The digit sum is between 2 and 18, so it is 4, 9 or 16. Sum 4: 13, 22, 31, 40 (4 numbers). Sum 9: 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81, 90 (9 numbers). Sum 16: 79, 88, 97 (3 numbers). Total $4+9+3=16$.

**Answer: (C) 16**

samf-junior-2000-r2-09.title: Prime factors
samf-junior-2000-r2-09.body:
$990=2\times3^2\times5\times11$. The prime 11 only appears in $n!$ once $n\ge11$, and $11!$ contains $2,3^2,5$ as well (e.g. $3,6$ give $3^2$). Since $10!$ has no factor 11, the smallest $n$ is 11.

**Answer: (C) 11**

samf-junior-2000-r2-10.title: Paint per square metre
samf-junior-2000-r2-10.body:
The cube has surface area $6\times4=24\text{ m}^2$, so 12 litres cover 24 m$^2$: half a litre per m$^2$. The box has surface area $2(4\cdot1+1\cdot8+4\cdot8)=2(44)=88\text{ m}^2$, so it needs $44$ litres.

**Answer: (B) 44**

samf-junior-2000-r2-11.title: Equation
samf-junior-2000-r2-11.body:
Let $k$ be the number of tests before the last. Then $\frac{89k+97}{k+1}=90$, so $89k+97=90k+90$ and $k=7$. With the last test she wrote $8$ tests.

**Answer: (E) 8**

samf-junior-2000-r2-11.title: Excess over the average
samf-junior-2000-r2-11.body:
The last mark is $97-90=7$ points above the new average. These 7 points make up for the $90-89=1$ point deficit of each of the earlier tests, so there were 7 earlier tests and $7+1=8$ in all.

**Answer: (E) 8**

samf-junior-2000-r2-12.title: Add angles
samf-junior-2000-r2-12.body:
$\angle ACB=45^\circ$ (diagonal of a square) and $\angle BCE=60^\circ$ (equilateral triangle). These angles are adjacent, so $\angle ACE=45^\circ+60^\circ=105^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) $105^\circ$**

samf-junior-2000-r2-13.title: Compute the new side
samf-junior-2000-r2-13.body:
Let the small hexagon have side 1 and centre O. Take a vertex V of the small hexagon and the side VU. Extending the side beyond V by 1 gives a new vertex W. Triangle OVU is equilateral, so $\angle OVU=60^\circ$ and $\angle OVW=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$. By the cosine rule $OW^2=1+1-2\cdot1\cdot1\cdot\cos120^\circ=3$. So the big regular hexagon has side $\sqrt3$ and areas are in the ratio $1:3$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac13$**

samf-junior-2000-r2-14.title: Venn diagram
samf-junior-2000-r2-14.body:
Let $a,b,c$ be the numbers watching exactly Monday and Tuesday, Monday and Wednesday, Tuesday and Wednesday. Monday: $11+a+b+7=25$, so $a+b=7$. Tuesday: $7+a+c+7=20$, so $a+c=6$. Wednesday: $6+b+c+7=16$, so $b+c=3$. Adding: $2(a+b+c)=16$, so exactly two days: 8. Total $=(11+7+6)+8+7=39$.

**Answer: (D) 39**

samf-junior-2000-r2-15.title: Pythagoras
samf-junior-2000-r2-15.body:
If the side is $s$, then $s^2+s^2=d^2$, so the area is $s^2=\frac12d^2$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac12d^2$**

samf-junior-2000-r2-15.title: Four triangles
samf-junior-2000-r2-15.body:
The square on the diagonal consists of 4 congruent right triangles while the original square has 2 of them. So the area of the original square is half the area $d^2$ of that square.

**Answer: (A) $\frac12d^2$**

samf-junior-2000-r2-16.title: Even and odd cases
samf-junior-2000-r2-16.body:
If $n=2k$, then $n^2=4k^2$ is a multiple of 4 while $n^2-1=4k^2-1$ is odd. If $n=2m-1$, then $n^2=4m^2-4m+1$ is odd while $n^2-1=4m(m-1)$ is a multiple of 4. So exactly one of the two is a multiple of 4. The other statements fail: one is odd and the other even, so (A), (B), (C) fail and the sum $2n^2-1$ is odd, so (E) fails.

**Answer: (D)**

samf-junior-2000-r2-17.title: Equation in whole numbers
samf-junior-2000-r2-17.body:
Let Pam eat $P_M$ on Monday and $P_T$ on Tuesday. All sweets eaten: $\frac74P_M+\frac53P_T=31$. For Sam's numbers to be whole, $P_M=4a$ and $P_T=3b$ with $7a+5b=31$. Trying $a=1,2,3,4$: only $a=3,b=2$ works. So Pam ate 12 and 6, and Sam ate $\frac34\cdot12+\frac23\cdot6=9+4=13$.

**Answer: (E) 13**

samf-junior-2000-r2-18.title: Times differ by 30 minutes
samf-junior-2000-r2-18.body:
Let the distance be $x$ km. Then $\frac x{27}-\frac x{36}=\frac{30}{60}=\frac12$ hour. So $\frac{4x-3x}{108}=\frac12$, $x=54$ km.

**Answer: (A) 54**

samf-junior-2000-r2-18.title: Use the ratio of speeds
samf-junior-2000-r2-18.body:
The speeds are in ratio $36:27=4:3$, so the times are in ratio $3:4$. The 30 minute difference is one part, so the faster journey takes $3\times30=90$ minutes $=1.5$ hours: distance $=36\times1.5=54$ km.

**Answer: (A) 54**

samf-junior-2000-r2-19.title: Follow the mark
samf-junior-2000-r2-19.body:
At the start the mark is at the top of the coin, where it moves forward fastest, so its path starts out horizontal. It comes down to the line after half a revolution, where it is momentarily at rest and moving straight down, then goes up again. This gives a cycloid, with a sharp point (cusp) on the line in the middle, as in (C). (A) and (B) do not have the right shape (a smooth dip or straight lines), (E) is a straight line, and (D) has a loop, which happens only for a mark beyond the rim.

**Answer: (C)**

samf-junior-2000-r2-20.title: Case analysis
samf-junior-2000-r2-20.body:
Statements I and II cannot both be true, so one of them is the false statement, and III and IV are both true. In particular IV is true. (It is possible: digit 1 makes I, III, IV true and II false; digit 2 likewise.)

**Answer: (E) IV is true.**
